processing: Made the way sheng pu-erh usually is: wilted, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried into maocha, then sold loose or pressed without ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: As with other Xishuangbanna sheng, spring picking is the prized one; autumn leaf is usually cheaper.
appearance_dry: Typical of sun-dried Yunnan leaf: long dark-green strands with paler downy buds.
appearance_liquor: In young tea, typically a clear pale gold.
appearance_wet: Typically thick olive-green leaves that open fully when the tea is young.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this tea's own flavour. Expect the general shape of young Menghai mountain sheng: some bitterness, a mineral edge and a sweet return in the throat.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Start short, as with any young sheng, and lengthen only once the bitterness settles.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like all sheng pu-erh, usually young and from the spring picking. A published spring price index listed small-tree leaf at 300 yuan per kilogram and old-tree leaf at 900 to 1,200, so the tree age on the label matters. The name is used loosely, so ask which village the leaf came from.
description:
Huazhu Liangzi is the highest peak of the Mengsong tea mountain, called the rooftop of Xishuangbanna, and the name has become a label for sheng from around it. The peak takes its name from a local clumping wild bamboo, the huazhu.

Strictly, the tea belongs to Baming, an Aini village northwest of Baotang whose old garden is the highest and closest to the summit. Its garden runs into Baotang's, and the two together are called the Huazhu Liangzi big tea garden.

The making is nothing unusual for sheng, so the place is the whole point. Little is documented about how this tea differs in the cup, so treat it as young Menghai mountain tea at first: short steeps, near-boiling water, and patience with the early bitterness.

When buying, ask for the village. Merchants once sold this leaf under the Baotang name because Baotang was better known, and more recently the fashion has run the other way, with teas from several neighbouring villages sold as Huazhu Liangzi.
history:
Mengsong was known first through Naka and Baotang. Baotang's old trees are the sturdiest in the area and made their name early, but that leaf is scarce, so traders long sold nearby tea as Baotang.

Only in recent years, with online tea talk and tighter market competition, did the other villages get names of their own, and many of their teas came to be grouped together as Huazhu Liangzi. No date for the first use of the name as a tea label is documented.
